```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var root = document.getElementById("w-alias"); if (!root) return;
  var cv = root.querySelector("#wa-canvas"), sn = root.querySelector("#wa-n"), sN = root.querySelector("#wa-N"),
      sf = root.querySelector("#wa-f"), out = root.querySelector("#wa-out");
  function css(n) { return getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue(n).trim() || "#888"; }
  function draw() {
    var n = parseInt(sn.value, 10), N = parseInt(sN.value, 10), f = sf.value;
    root.querySelector("#wa-nv").textContent = n; root.querySelector("#wa-Nv").textContent = N;
    var m = ((n % N) + N) % N; if (m > N / 2) m -= N;          // representative in (-N/2, N/2]
    var am = Math.abs(m), sgn = (f === "sin" && m < 0) ? -1 : 1;
    var nyq = (N % 2 === 0 && am === N / 2);
    var dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1, W = cv.clientWidth || 720, H = Math.round(W * 300 / 720);
    cv.width = Math.round(W * dpr); cv.height = Math.round(H * dpr);
    var g = cv.getContext("2d"); g.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
    var bg = css("--bg"), ink = css("--ink"), mut = css("--hair"), c1 = css("--mw-c1"), c2 = css("--mw-c2");
    g.fillStyle = bg; g.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    var pad = 14, X = function (x) { return pad + x / (2 * Math.PI) * (W - 2 * pad); }, Y = function (y) { return H / 2 - y * (H / 2 - pad - 4); };
    g.strokeStyle = mut; g.lineWidth = 1; g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(0), Y(0)); g.lineTo(X(2 * Math.PI), Y(0)); g.stroke();
    var fn = function (k, x) { return f === "cos" ? Math.cos(k * x) : Math.sin(k * x); };
    g.strokeStyle = c1; g.lineWidth = 1.3; g.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= 1400; i++) { var x = 2 * Math.PI * i / 1400, y = fn(n, x); if (i) g.lineTo(X(x), Y(y)); else g.moveTo(X(x), Y(y)); }
    g.stroke();
    g.strokeStyle = c2; g.lineWidth = 3; g.beginPath();
    for (i = 0; i <= 700; i++) { x = 2 * Math.PI * i / 700; y = sgn * fn(am, x); if (nyq && f === "sin") y = 0; if (i) g.lineTo(X(x), Y(y)); else g.moveTo(X(x), Y(y)); }
    g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle = ink; g.strokeStyle = bg; g.lineWidth = 2;
    for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) { x = 2 * Math.PI * j / N; y = fn(n, x); g.beginPath(); g.arc(X(x), Y(y), 5.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); g.fill(); g.stroke(); }
    var resolu = n < N / 2;
    var txt = "Nyquist wavenumber: N/2 = " + String(N / 2) + ". ";
    if (resolu) txt += "The mode n = " + n + " is resolved: it is its own representative.";
    else if (n === N / 2) txt += "The mode n = " + n + " is the Nyquist mode: " + (f === "cos" ? "cos(" + n + " x) equals ±1 at the grid points; it is represented, but its derivative is not (Definition 5.11)." : "sin(" + n + " x) vanishes at every grid point: it is invisible.");
    else txt +="The mode n = " + n + " is not resolved: on the grid, " + f + "(" + n + " x) coincides with " +
      (nyq && f === "sin" ? "0 (Nyquist mode: sin vanishes at every point)" : (sgn < 0 ? "−" : "") + f + "(" + am + " x)") + ", because " + n + " ≡ " + m + " (mod " + N + ").";
    out.textContent = txt;
  }
  [sn, sN].forEach(function (s) { s.addEventListener("input", draw); }); sf.addEventListener("change", draw);
  window.addEventListener("resize", draw);
  new MutationObserver(draw).observe(document.documentElement, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-theme"] });
  if (window.matchMedia) { var mq = window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"); if (mq.addEventListener) mq.addEventListener("change", draw); }
  draw();
})();
</script>
```

### 5.3 The fast Fourier transform (FFT)

Computing the $N$ coefficients from the definition costs $N^2$ operations. The Cooley–Tukey algorithm (1965) reduces this cost to $O(N\log N)$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.10 — Even–odd splitting (Cooley–Tukey)]{.tag}
Let $N$ be even, $w = e^{-2i\pi/N}$ and $F_n = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f_j w^{jn}$. Let $E_n$ and $O_n$ denote the (unnormalized) DFTs of size $N/2$ of the samples with even and odd indices. Then, for $n = 0, \dots, N/2 - 1$:

$$
F_n = E_n + w^n O_n, \qquad F_{n + N/2} = E_n - w^n O_n.
$$

::: proof
We separate $j = 2m$ and $j = 2m+1$: $F_n = \sum_m f_{2m}(w^2)^{mn} + w^n\sum_m f_{2m+1}(w^2)^{mn}$. Now $w^2 = e^{-2i\pi/(N/2)}$ is the root of unity of order $N/2$: the two sums are $E_n$ and $O_n$. The latter are $N/2$-periodic in $n$ and $w^{N/2} = -1$, which gives the second formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If $C(N)$ is the cost for a size $N = 2^q$, then $C(N) = 2C(N/2) + O(N)$, hence $C(N) = O(N\log_2 N)$. For a 3D grid of $256^3 = 2^{24}$ points, the ratio between $N^2 \approx 2.8\times 10^{14}$ and $N\log_2 N \approx 4.0\times 10^{8}$ is about $7\times 10^5$: without the FFT, spectral methods would be unusable. Multiple dimensions are handled axis by axis (`np.fft.fftn`).

### 5.4 Spectral differentiation

::: def
[Definition 5.11 — Spectral derivative]{.tag}
The spectral derivative of $(f_j)$ is the vector

$$
(D_N f)_j = \sum_{n}ik_n\,\hat f_n\,e^{ik_n x_j},
$$

that is, the exact derivative of the trigonometric polynomial that interpolates $f$ at the grid points. For even $N$, $ik_{N/2}$ is replaced by $0$: the Nyquist mode $\cos(\frac{N}{2}x)$ has a derivative $-\frac N2\sin(\frac N2 x)$ that vanishes on the grid, and keeping it would give a non-real derivative (Trefethen, 2000).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.12 — Accuracy of the spectral derivative]{.tag}
If $\sum_n|k_n\hat f_n|$ converges, the error at the grid points satisfies

$$
\max_j\big|(D_N f)_j - f'(x_j)\big| \le 2\sum_{|n|\ge N/2}|k_n|\,|\hat f_n|.
$$

If $|\hat f_n| = O(|n|^{-q})$ with $q > 2$, the error is therefore $O(N^{2-q})$; if $f$ is analytic, the coefficients decay exponentially and so does the error (**spectral convergence**).

::: proof
Sketch. $f'(x_j) = \sum_m ik_m\hat f_m e^{ik_m x_j}$, while $D_N f$ uses the folded coefficients (5.2) multiplied by $ik_n$ with $|n| < N/2$. The difference consists of the modes $|m| \ge N/2$ of $f'$, whose sum is bounded by $\sum_{|m|\ge N/2}|k_m||\hat f_m|$, and of the folded terms $ik_n\hat f_{n+pN}$ with $p \neq 0$, where $|k_n| < |k_{n+pN}|$: their sum is bounded by the same quantity. The Nyquist mode set to zero falls under the same count. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The code below compares the spectral derivative with second-order centered finite differences for $f = e^{\sin x}$, an analytic function, then checks Parseval and measures the Gibbs phenomenon.

```python
import numpy as np

def nombres_onde(N, L=2 * np.pi):
    """k_n = 2 pi n / L in the np.fft order (0, 1, ..., N/2-1, -N/2, ..., -1)."""
    return 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L / N)

def derivee_spectrale(f, L=2 * np.pi):
    N = f.size
    k = nombres_onde(N, L)
    if N % 2 == 0:
        k[N // 2] = 0.0          # Nyquist mode: odd derivative set to zero
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft(1j * k * np.fft.fft(f)))

def derivee_df2(f, L=2 * np.pi):  # second-order centered finite differences
    h = L / f.size
    return (np.roll(f, -1) - np.roll(f, 1)) / (2 * h)

print(" N   spectral error     FD order 2 error")
for N in [8, 16, 32, 64, 128]:
    x = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N) / N
    f, fp = np.exp(np.sin(x)), np.cos(x) * np.exp(np.sin(x))
    e_s = np.abs(derivee_spectrale(f) - fp).max()
    e_d = np.abs(derivee_df2(f) - fp).max()
    print(f"{N:3d}   {e_s:.1e}            {e_d:.1e}")

# Discrete Parseval: (1/N) sum |f_j|^2 = sum |f^_k|^2 with f^_k = fft(f)/N
N = 64
x = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N) / N
f = np.exp(np.sin(x))
fh = np.fft.fft(f) / N
print("Parseval :", f"{np.mean(f**2):.15f}", f"{np.sum(np.abs(fh)**2):.15f}")

# Gibbs: partial sums of the square wave sign(sin x) = (4/pi) sum_{n odd} sin(n x)/n
xx = np.linspace(1e-4, np.pi / 2, 200001)
for n_max in [11, 101, 1001]:
    S = sum(4 / np.pi * np.sin(n * xx) / n for n in range(1, n_max + 1, 2))
    print(f"n_max = {n_max:4d} : max of the partial sum = {S.max():.4f}")
# output:
#  N   spectral error     FD order 2 error
#   8   4.3e-03            3.4e-01
#  16   1.8e-07            9.4e-02
#  32   2.9e-15            2.6e-02
#  64   1.1e-14            6.5e-03
# 128   2.4e-14            1.6e-03
# Parseval : 2.279585302336067 2.279585302336067
# n_max =   11 : max of the partial sum = 1.1813
# n_max =  101 : max of the partial sum = 1.1790
# n_max = 1001 : max of the partial sum = 1.1790
```

With 32 points, the spectral derivative reaches machine precision, whereas second-order finite differences still make an error of a few percent and gain only a factor of 4 each time $N$ doubles. The slight rise of the spectral error beyond $N = 32$ is due to rounding, which grows like $N\epsilon_{\text{machine}}$ because the wavenumbers multiply the errors. The maximum of the partial sums of the square wave settles at $1.1790$: the Gibbs overshoot does not disappear when modes are added, it only becomes narrower against the jump.

![Three phenomena of this chapter. Left, aliasing: on the grid of $N = 8$ points, $\cos(10x)$ and $\cos(2x)$ take the same values. Center, the Gibbs phenomenon: the partial sums of the square wave overshoot the value 1 by about $0.179$ near the jump, for $n_{\max} = 11$ as well as for $n_{\max} = 101$. Right, the maximum error of the derivative of $e^{\sin x}$: exponential decay for the spectral method down to rounding, as $N^{-2}$ for second-order finite differences.](../../../prep/p1-calcul-vectoriel/fig-fourier-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Three plots. First: a fast sinusoid and a slow one pass through the same eight black dots. Second: two partial sums of a square wave oscillate near the jump at x = 0 and overshoot the value 1 up to about 1.18. Third: on a logarithmic scale, the spectral error drops from 1e-1 to 1e-15 between N = 6 and N = 32 and then rises slightly, while the finite-difference error decreases along a straight line of slope -2." }

### 5.5 Fourier in several dimensions and energy spectrum

In a periodic box $[0, L)^3$, the wave vectors are $\mathbf{k} \in \frac{2\pi}{L}\mathbb{Z}^3$ and a field is written $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$. The operators become algebraic:

$$
\widehat{\nabla f} = i\mathbf{k}\hat f, \qquad \widehat{\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}} = i\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}, \qquad \widehat{\nabla\times\mathbf{u}} = i\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}, \qquad \widehat{\Delta f} = -|\mathbf{k}|^2\hat f.
$$

The identities of Chapter 2 become identities between vectors: $\mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}) = 0$, and $i\mathbf{k}\times(i\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}) = -\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}) + |\mathbf{k}|^2\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, which is nothing but the vector triple product formula $\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})$.

::: def
[Definition 5.13 — Energy and helicity spectra]{.tag}
For $L = 2\pi$, the shell energy spectrum is

$$
E(K) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{K - 1/2 \,\le\, |\mathbf{k}| \,<\, K + 1/2}|\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}|^2, \qquad K = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

By Parseval, $\sum_K E(K) = \frac12\langle|\mathbf{u}|^2\rangle$ (provided all the shells are counted). The kinetic helicity spectrum is defined in the same way with $\operatorname{Re}\big(\overline{\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}_{\mathbf{k}}\big)$ in place of $\frac12|\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}|^2$.
:::

::: note
[Remark 5.14 — Discrete consistency]{.tag}
On a grid, the identities $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{u}) = 0$ or $\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{u}) = \nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}) - \Delta\mathbf{u}$ are exact (up to rounding) only if **all** the operators use the same wavenumbers. With the Nyquist convention of Definition 5.11, the Laplacian must therefore be computed as $-|\mathbf{k}|^2$ with these same modified $\mathbf{k}$; otherwise the identity is false on the Nyquist modes.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
N, L = 32, 2 * np.pi
kv = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L / N)       # true wavenumbers
filtre = np.exp(-sum(k**2 for k in np.meshgrid(kv, kv, kv, indexing="ij")) / 16)
k1 = kv.copy(); k1[N // 2] = 0.0                   # Nyquist set to zero (odd derivatives)
KX, KY, KZ = np.meshgrid(k1, k1, k1, indexing="ij")
K = np.stack([KX, KY, KZ])                         # wave vector, shape (3, N, N, N)
K2 = (K**2).sum(0)                                 # |k|^2 consistent with this choice

F  = lambda a: np.fft.fftn(a, axes=(-3, -2, -1))
Fi = lambda a: np.real(np.fft.ifftn(a, axes=(-3, -2, -1)))
grad = lambda f: Fi(1j * K * F(f))
div  = lambda u: Fi((1j * K * F(u)).sum(0))
def rot(u):
    uh = F(u)
    return Fi(1j * np.stack([K[1]*uh[2] - K[2]*uh[1],
                             K[2]*uh[0] - K[0]*uh[2],
                             K[0]*uh[1] - K[1]*uh[0]]))
lap = lambda u: Fi(-K2 * F(u))

def lisse(shape):                                   # filtered white noise, then normalized
    a = Fi(F(rng.normal(size=shape)) * filtre)
    return a / a.std()

u, f = lisse((3, N, N, N)), lisse((N, N, N))
print("max|rot grad f|          =", f"{np.abs(rot(grad(f))).max():.1e}", " (max|grad f| =", f"{np.abs(grad(f)).max():.1e})")
print("max|div rot u|           =", f"{np.abs(div(rot(u))).max():.1e}", " (max|rot u|  =", f"{np.abs(rot(u)).max():.1e})")
e = rot(rot(u)) - (grad(div(u)) - lap(u))
print("max|rot rot u - (grad div u - lap u)| =", f"{np.abs(e).max():.1e}")

# Parseval in 3D: <|u|^2> = sum_k |u^_k|^2 with u^_k = fft(u)/N^3
uh = F(u) / N**3
print("Parseval : <|u|^2> =", f"{np.mean((u**2).sum(0)):.12f}", "; sum|u^_k|^2 =", f"{np.sum(np.abs(uh)**2):.12f}")

# ABC flow: shell energy spectrum and kinetic helicity
x = L * np.arange(N) / N
X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(x, x, x, indexing="ij")
A, B, C = 1.0, 0.8, 0.6
v = np.stack([A*np.sin(Z) + C*np.cos(Y), B*np.sin(X) + A*np.cos(Z), C*np.sin(Y) + B*np.cos(X)])
vh = F(v) / N**3
kn = np.sqrt(K2)
E = [0.5 * np.sum(np.abs(vh)**2 * ((kn >= s - 0.5) & (kn < s + 0.5))) for s in range(4)]
print("spectrum E(k), k = 0..3 :", np.round(E, 12), "; (A^2+B^2+C^2)/2 =", (A*A + B*B + C*C) / 2)
print("helicity <u . rot u> =", f"{np.mean((v * rot(v)).sum(0)):.12f}", "; A^2+B^2+C^2 =", A*A + B*B + C*C)
# output:
# max|rot grad f|          = 2.8e-14  (max|grad f| = 1.0e+01)
# max|div rot u|           = 4.5e-14  (max|rot u|  = 1.2e+01)
# max|rot rot u - (grad div u - lap u)| = 5.6e-14
# Parseval : <|u|^2> = 3.007055058030 ; sum|u^_k|^2 = 3.007055058030
# spectrum E(k), k = 0..3 : [0. 1. 0. 0.] ; (A^2+B^2+C^2)/2 = 1.0
# helicity <u . rot u> = 2.000000000000 ; A^2+B^2+C^2 = 2.0
```

The identities are satisfied to within about $10^{-15}$ relative to the size of the terms. All the energy of the ABC flow lies in the shell $K = 1$, and its mean helicity is indeed $A^2 + B^2 + C^2 = 2$.

### 5.6 Products, aliasing and the 2/3 rule

Nonlinear terms, such as $(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}$ or $\nabla\times(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B})$, are computed in pseudo-spectral codes by pointwise multiplication on the grid, which costs only $O(N)$ operations after the FFTs. But a product widens the spectrum.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.15 — Spectrum of a product]{.tag}
The Fourier coefficients of a product are the convolution of the coefficients: $\widehat{(uv)}_n = \sum_{p + q = n}\hat u_p\hat v_q$. If $u$ and $v$ have only modes $|n| \le K$, their product has modes up to $|n| = 2K$.

::: proof
We expand $uv = \sum_{p,q}\hat u_p\hat v_q e^{i(k_p + k_q)x}$ and group the terms according to $n = p + q$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.16 — The 2/3 rule (Orszag, 1971)]{.tag}
If $\hat u$ and $\hat v$ are truncated at $|n| \le K$ with $N \ge 3K + 1$, then the DFT coefficients of the product computed on the grid coincide, for $|n| \le K$, with the exact coefficients of $uv$.

::: proof
By (5.2), the DFT coefficient of the product equals $\sum_p\widehat{(uv)}_{n + pN}$. The exact product has only modes $|m| \le 2K$. For $|n| \le K$ and $p \neq 0$, we have $|n + pN| \ge N - |n| \ge N - K \ge 2K + 1$: all the folded terms vanish. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In practice, the fields are kept truncated at $|n| \le N/3$ by setting the modes $|n| > N/3$ to zero after each product, so that the factors of the next product are truncated too: only the central two thirds of the spectrum are kept, hence the name of the rule. The following code shows aliasing and then its elimination.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

# 1) Aliasing: cos(10 x) sampled on N = 8 points coincides with cos(2 x)
N = 8
x = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N) / N
print("max|cos(10x) - cos(2x)| on the grid N=8 :", f"{np.abs(np.cos(10*x) - np.cos(2*x)).max():.1e}")

# 2) Product u*u computed "pseudo-spectrally" on a grid of N points
N = 32
k = np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=1 / N)                     # integers 0..15, -16..-1

def champ_aleatoire(K):
    """Real field whose modes satisfy 1 <= |k| <= K."""
    uh = np.zeros(N, complex)
    for n in range(1, K + 1):
        c = rng.normal() + 1j * rng.normal()
        uh[n], uh[-n] = c, np.conj(c)
    return uh                                       # coefficients (fft/N convention)

def produit_exact(uh, vh):
    """Exact coefficients of u*v for |k| < N/2: direct discrete convolution."""
    wh = np.zeros(N, complex)
    for p in range(N):
        for q in range(N):
            s = k[p] + k[q]
            if abs(s) < N / 2:
                wh[int(s) % N] += uh[p] * vh[q]
    return wh

def produit_grille(uh, vh):                         # pointwise product
    u, v = np.fft.ifft(uh * N), np.fft.ifft(vh * N)
    return np.fft.fft(u * v) / N

uh = champ_aleatoire(15)                            # all modes resolved
err = np.abs(produit_grille(uh, uh) - produit_exact(uh, uh))
print("no precaution : max error on the coefficients of u^2 =", f"{err.max():.2f}",
      "(size of the coefficients ~", f"{np.abs(produit_exact(uh, uh)).max():.1f})")

K = N // 3                                          # 2/3 rule: |k| <= 10
garde = np.abs(k) <= K
uh2 = uh * garde                                    # truncate u before the product
err = np.abs((produit_grille(uh2, uh2) - produit_exact(uh2, uh2))[garde])
print("2/3 rule      : max error on the modes |k| <= 10 =", f"{err.max():.1e}")
# output:
# max|cos(10x) - cos(2x)| on the grid N=8 : 3.5e-15
# no precaution : max error on the coefficients of u^2 = 12.50 (size of the coefficients ~ 77.5)
# 2/3 rule      : max error on the modes |k| <= 10 = 1.1e-14
```

Without precaution, the aliased modes pollute the coefficients of the product with an error that reaches about 16% of the largest coefficient; with truncation to two thirds, the error drops to rounding. In a simulation, this aliasing injects spurious energy at small scales and can make the computation blow up.

::: note
[Remark 5.17 — Discontinuities and filtering]{.tag}
The Gibbs phenomenon is a problem as soon as the coefficients of the problem are discontinuous. In the LATU code, the VKS impellers are represented by penalization in a periodic box, with a magnetic permeability that jumps at their surface; to limit the Gibbs oscillations, Kreuzahler et al. (2017) filter these jumps with a *sharpened raised cosine* filter.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::
- In Fourier space, $\partial_x \to ik$, $\nabla \to i\mathbf{k}$, $\Delta \to -|\mathbf{k}|^2$; Parseval identifies the mean energy with the sum of the modal energies, hence the spectrum $E(K)$.
- The smoothness of a function can be read in the decay of its coefficients; the spectral derivative converges exponentially for an analytic function.
- On $N$ points, the modes $n$ and $n + N$ are confused (aliasing); the Nyquist mode requires a consistent convention for all derivatives.
- The FFT costs $O(N\log N)$; products double the width of the spectrum, and the 2/3 rule ($N \ge 3K + 1$) eliminates the aliasing of quadratic terms.
::::

## 6. Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition and Leray projection {#ch6}

A field produced by a numerical scheme or by a generative network generally has a small nonzero divergence. The Helmholtz–Hodge theorem states that every field decomposes uniquely into a gradient part and a solenoidal part; keeping only the latter is called **projecting**. In a periodic box, this projection costs two FFTs (forward and backward) and a small matrix–vector multiplication per wave vector. With walls, it requires solving a global elliptic problem. This contrast lies at the heart of the modeling choices of the internship.

### 6.1 General statement

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.1 — Helmholtz–Hodge in a bounded domain (statement)]{.tag}
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded, connected domain with smooth boundary and outward normal $\mathbf{n}$. Every square-integrable field $\mathbf{u}$ on $\Omega$ decomposes uniquely as

$$
\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w} + \nabla p, \qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{w} = 0 \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,
$$

where $p$ is defined up to a constant. The two parts are orthogonal in $L^2(\Omega)$: $\int_\Omega\mathbf{w}\cdot\nabla p\,\mathrm{d}V = 0$. The potential $p$ solves the **Neumann problem**

$$
\Delta p = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} \ \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad \partial_n p = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{n} \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega. \tag{6.1}
$$

::: proof
Let us prove orthogonality and uniqueness; existence relies on solving (6.1), which is taken for granted here (see Chorin and Marsden, 1993, or Girault and Raviart, 1986). By (3.3), $\int_\Omega\mathbf{w}\cdot\nabla p = \oint_{\partial\Omega}p\,\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{n} - \int_\Omega p\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{w} = 0$. If $\mathbf{w}_1 + \nabla p_1 = \mathbf{w}_2 + \nabla p_2$, the field $\mathbf{w}_1 - \mathbf{w}_2 = \nabla(p_2 - p_1)$ is both solenoidal with zero normal flux and a gradient: it is orthogonal to itself, hence zero. Finally, taking the divergence and the normal component of $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w} + \nabla p$ gives (6.1). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Compatibility of the Neumann problem]{.tag}
The problem $\Delta p = f$ in $\Omega$, $\partial_n p = g$ on $\partial\Omega$ can have a solution only if $\int_\Omega f\,\mathrm{d}V = \oint_{\partial\Omega}g\,\mathrm{d}S$, and two solutions differ by a constant. For (6.1), the condition is automatically satisfied.

::: proof
The necessary condition is Theorem 3.5 applied to $\nabla p$. For (6.1), it is again Theorem 3.5, applied to $\mathbf{u}$. If $q$ is the difference of two solutions, $\Delta q = 0$ and $\partial_n q = 0$, and Green's identity gives $\int_\Omega|\nabla q|^2 = \oint_{\partial\Omega}q\,\partial_n q - \int_\Omega q\,\Delta q = 0$, so $q$ is constant on the connected domain. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — The projection is the minimal correction]{.tag}
Write $\mathbf{w} = \mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$ for the solenoidal part. For every solenoidal field $\mathbf{v}$ satisfying $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$ on the boundary:

$$
\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}\|_{L^2} \le \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_{L^2}.
$$

::: proof
$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \nabla p + (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{v})$, and $\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{v}$ is solenoidal with zero normal flux, hence orthogonal to $\nabla p$. By Pythagoras, $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\nabla p\|^2 + \|\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 \ge \|\nabla p\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{w}\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Projecting a generated field therefore amounts to modifying it as little as possible, in the energy sense, to satisfy the constraint. This does not guarantee that the projected field is physically plausible: the removed gradient part may contain useful information, and the projection may modify the statistics (spectrum, helicity) of the generated field.

### 6.2 Proof in a periodic box

On the periodic torus $\mathbb{T}^d = [0, L)^d$, there is no boundary, and Fourier diagonalizes everything.

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Helmholtz–Hodge on the torus]{.tag}
Every real square-integrable field $\mathbf{u}$ on $\mathbb{T}^d$ decomposes uniquely as

$$
\mathbf{u} = \bar{\mathbf{u}} + \nabla p + \mathbf{w},
$$

where $\bar{\mathbf{u}} = \langle\mathbf{u}\rangle$ is constant, $p$ is periodic with zero mean, and $\mathbf{w}$ is periodic, solenoidal and with zero mean. The three parts are pairwise orthogonal. In Fourier space, for $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$:

$$
\hat p_{\mathbf{k}} = -i\,\frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}} - \mathbf{k}\,\frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} = \Big(I - \frac{\mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}^{\mathsf{T}}}{|\mathbf{k}|^2}\Big)\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}. \tag{6.2}
$$

::: proof
*Existence.* We define $\hat p_{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ by (6.2) for $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$, and $\hat p_{\mathbf{0}} = 0$, $\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{0}} = \mathbf{0}$. Then $\widehat{\nabla p}_{\mathbf{k}} = i\mathbf{k}\hat p_{\mathbf{k}} = \mathbf{k}(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}})/|\mathbf{k}|^2$, so that $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \widehat{\nabla p}_{\mathbf{k}} + \hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ for $\mathbf{k}\neq\mathbf{0}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{0}} = \bar{\mathbf{u}}$. We check that $i\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}} = i\big(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}} - |\mathbf{k}|^2\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}/|\mathbf{k}|^2\big) = 0$. Since $\mathbf{u}$ is real, $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{-\mathbf{k}} = \overline{\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}}$. The matrix $I - \mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}^{\mathsf{T}}/|\mathbf{k}|^2$ is real and even in $\mathbf{k}$, so $\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{-\mathbf{k}} = \overline{\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}}}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ is real. For $p$, the factor $\mathbf{k}$ changes sign with $\mathbf{k}$ and the factor $-i$ changes sign under conjugation: $\hat p_{-\mathbf{k}} = \overline{\hat p_{\mathbf{k}}}$, and $p$ is real as well. Finally, $|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}}| \le |\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}|$ and $|\mathbf{k}\hat p_{\mathbf{k}}| \le |\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}|$, so that the series converge in $L^2$.

*Orthogonality.* By Parseval (in its polarized form $\langle\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\rangle = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}\overline{\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\mathbf{k}}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ for real fields),

$$
\langle\nabla p\cdot\mathbf{w}\rangle = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}\overline{i\mathbf{k}\hat p_{\mathbf{k}}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}(-i)\,\overline{\hat p_{\mathbf{k}}}\,(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathbf{k}}) = 0.
$$

The constant field is orthogonal to the other two, which have zero mean.

*Uniqueness.* Consider a decomposition of zero, $\bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla q + \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0}$. The mode $\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $\bar{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}$. For $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$, the dot product with $\mathbf{k}$ gives $i|\mathbf{k}|^2\hat q_{\mathbf{k}} + \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathbf{k}} = i|\mathbf{k}|^2\hat q_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$, hence $\hat q_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$, and then $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \mathbf{0}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Leray projector]{.tag}
The Leray projector, named after the mathematician who introduced weak solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations (Leray, 1934), is the operator $\mathbb{P}$ that acts in Fourier space by $\widehat{(\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u})}_{\mathbf{k}} = P(\mathbf{k})\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}$, with

$$
P_{ij}(\mathbf{k}) = \delta_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} \quad (\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}), \qquad P(\mathbf{0}) = I.
$$

With this convention, $\mathbb{P}$ preserves the mean field and removes the gradient part.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — Properties of the Leray projector on the torus]{.tag}
(i) $\mathbb{P}^2 = \mathbb{P}$; (ii) $\mathbb{P}$ is symmetric: $\langle\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\rangle = \langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbb{P}\mathbf{v}\rangle$; (iii) $\langle|\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}|^2\rangle \le \langle|\mathbf{u}|^2\rangle$; (iv) $\nabla\cdot\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u} = 0$; (v) $\mathbb{P}$ commutes with derivatives and with the Laplacian; (vi) $\mathbb{P}(\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbb{P}(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$.

::: proof
For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$, $P(\mathbf{k})$ is the matrix of the orthogonal projection onto the plane orthogonal to $\mathbf{k}$: $P(\mathbf{k})^2 = P(\mathbf{k})$ and $P(\mathbf{k})^{\mathsf{T}} = P(\mathbf{k})$. With Parseval, we obtain (i), (ii) and (iii). (iv): $\mathbf{k}\cdot P(\mathbf{k})\hat{\mathbf{u}} = 0$. (v): derivatives act in Fourier space by multiplication by scalars or vectors; for the divergence and the curl, one checks directly that $\mathbf{k}\cdot P(\mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{0}$ and that $\mathbf{k}\times P(\mathbf{k})\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}}$; the Laplacian is a scalar multiplier. (vi): $P(\mathbf{k})\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ is already orthogonal to $\mathbf{k}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For an isotropic random field (white noise, for example), each coefficient $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ has the same variance in the $d$ directions and the projection removes one of them: on average, a fraction $(d-1)/d$ of the energy is kept, that is $1/2$ in 2D and $2/3$ in 3D. In 2D, the projection can also be written with the stream function: $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u} = \bar{\mathbf{u}} + \nabla^\perp\psi$ with $-\Delta\psi = \omega$, where $\omega$ is the vorticity of $\mathbf{u}$ (Exercise 14).

![Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition of a smooth random field on the torus $[0, 2\pi)^2$ (computed with formula (6.2)). Left, the field $\mathbf{u}$ and, in the background, its divergence. Center, the gradient part $\nabla p$, without vorticity, whose streamlines, which climb along $p$, start from its minima (in blue) and converge toward its maxima (in red). Right, the solenoidal part $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$, without divergence, whose streamlines wind around the extrema of the vorticity. The thickness of the lines is proportional to the magnitude of the field.](../../../prep/p1-calcul-vectoriel/fig-helmholtz-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Three panels of streamlines on a colored background, linked by equals and plus signs. The first mixes sources, sinks and vortices; the second shows only sources and sinks; the third shows only vortices and closed lines."}

::: note
[Remark 6.7 — “Zero divergence” depends on the discrete operator]{.tag}
On a grid, $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$ computed by FFT has zero divergence to machine precision **if the divergence is measured with the same wavenumbers** (including the Nyquist convention). Measured by finite differences, the divergence of the same field is only $O(h^2)$, where $h$ is the grid spacing. A “divergence control” metric is therefore meaningful only if the discrete operator used is specified. With the Nyquist convention, the few modes all of whose modified wavenumbers vanish (the mean mode, but also the “pure” Nyquist modes, such as $(N/2, 0)$ or $(N/2, N/2)$ in 2D) are left untouched by the formula of Definition 6.5; one may prefer to set them to zero, as in Exercise 14.
:::

The following code projects white noises in 2D and 3D and checks the properties of Proposition 6.6.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

def vecteurs_onde(N, d, L=2 * np.pi):
    k1 = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L / N)
    k1[N // 2] = 0.0                       # same convention as for the derivatives
    return np.stack(np.meshgrid(*([k1] * d), indexing="ij"))

def leray(u, K):
    """Leray projection: u^_k <- u^_k - k (k . u^_k)/|k|^2 (mode k = 0 kept)."""
    ax = tuple(range(1, u.ndim))
    uh = np.fft.fftn(u, axes=ax)
    K2 = (K**2).sum(0)
    K2[K2 == 0] = 1.0                      # avoids 0/0; k.u^ = 0 at these points anyway
    uh = uh - K * (K * uh).sum(0) / K2
    return np.real(np.fft.ifftn(uh, axes=ax))

def divergence(u, K):
    ax = tuple(range(1, u.ndim))
    return np.real(np.fft.ifftn((1j * K * np.fft.fftn(u, axes=ax)).sum(0)))

for d, N in [(2, 256), (3, 64)]:
    K = vecteurs_onde(N, d)
    u = rng.normal(size=(d,) + (N,) * d)   # white noise: very far from solenoidal
    w = leray(u, K)
    g = u - w                              # gradient part
    a, b = divergence(u, K).std(), np.abs(divergence(w, K)).max()
    print(f"d = {d}, N = {N} : rms div u = {a:.1e} -> max|div Pu| = {b:.1e} "
          f"(ratio {b / a:.1e})")
    print(f"   ||P(Pu) - Pu||max = {np.abs(leray(w, K) - w).max():.1e} ; "
          f"<Pu . (u - Pu)> = {np.mean((w * g).sum(0)):.1e} ; "
          f"energy kept = {np.mean((w**2).sum(0)) / np.mean((u**2).sum(0)):.3f}")
# output:
# d = 2, N = 256 : rms div u = 1.0e+02 -> max|div Pu| = 9.5e-14 (ratio 9.1e-16)
#    ||P(Pu) - Pu||max = 8.9e-16 ; <Pu . (u - Pu)> = -3.7e-17 ; energy kept = 0.499
# d = 3, N = 64 : rms div u = 3.1e+01 -> max|div Pu| = 3.6e-14 (ratio 1.2e-15)
#    ||P(Pu) - Pu||max = 1.8e-15 ; <Pu . (u - Pu)> = -2.5e-16 ; energy kept = 0.667
```

The divergence goes from a typical value of 100 (white noise has a lot of energy at small scales) to about $10^{-15}$ times that value. The projection is idempotent, its two parts are orthogonal, and it keeps half of the energy in 2D and two thirds in 3D, as expected.

The following interactive diagram redoes this computation in the browser, on a $32\times 32$ grid, for a field whose scale is set by a Gaussian filter of width $k_c$ in wavenumber. It shows the two parts of the decomposition, and the three properties can be read on it: energies that add up, divergence of $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$ at the level of rounding, vorticity of $\nabla p$ at the same level.

```{=html}
(function () {
  var root = document.getElementById("w-leray"); if (!root) return;
  var cv = root.querySelector("#wl-canvas"), out = root.querySelector("#wl-out"), skc = root.querySelector("#wl-kc");
  var N = 32, seed = 7, state = null;
  function css(n) { return getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue(n).trim() || "#888"; }
  function rng(a) { return function () { a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0; var t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a); t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t; return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; }
  var CS = [], SN = [];
  for (var t = 0; t < N; t++) { CS.push(Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * t / N)); SN.push(Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * t / N)); }
  function dft1(re, im, inv) {                       // naive DFT of length N (forward: e^{-2iπjn/N})
    var R = new Float64Array(N), I = new Float64Array(N), s = inv ? 1 : -1;
    for (var n = 0; n < N; n++) { var a = 0, b = 0;
      for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) { var q = (j * n) % N, c = CS[q], d = s * SN[q]; a += re[j] * c - im[j] * d; b += re[j] * d + im[j] * c; }
      R[n] = inv ? a / N : a; I[n] = inv ? b / N : b; }
    return [R, I];
  }
  function dft2(re, im, inv) {                       // N*N arrays, index i*N + j (i: x, j: y)
    var R = new Float64Array(N * N), I = new Float64Array(N * N), a = new Float64Array(N), b = new Float64Array(N), i, j, r;
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) { for (j = 0; j < N; j++) { a[j] = re[i * N + j]; b[j] = im[i * N + j]; } r = dft1(a, b, inv); for (j = 0; j < N; j++) { R[i * N + j] = r[0][j]; I[i * N + j] = r[1][j]; } }
    for (j = 0; j < N; j++) { for (i = 0; i < N; i++) { a[i] = R[i * N + j]; b[i] = I[i * N + j]; } r = dft1(a, b, inv); for (i = 0; i < N; i++) { R[i * N + j] = r[0][i]; I[i * N + j] = r[1][i]; } }
    return [R, I];
  }
  function kk(i) { return i < N / 2 ? i : (i === N / 2 ? 0 : i - N); }   // wavenumbers, Nyquist set to zero
  function compute() {
    var kc = parseFloat(skc.value), r = rng(seed), z = new Float64Array(N * N), U = [];
    root.querySelector("#wl-kcv").textContent = kc.toFixed(1);
    for (var c = 0; c < 2; c++) {
      var a = new Float64Array(N * N);
      for (var p = 0; p < N * N; p++) { var u1 = r() || 1e-12, u2 = r(); a[p] = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u1)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * u2); }
      var h = dft2(a, z, false);
      for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) {
        var kx = i < N / 2 ? i : i - N, ky = j < N / 2 ? j : j - N, k2 = kx * kx + ky * ky, ny = (i === N / 2 || j === N / 2);
        var f = (k2 === 0 || ny) ? 0 : Math.exp(-k2 / (2 * kc * kc)); h[0][i * N + j] *= f; h[1][i * N + j] *= f;
      }
      U.push(h);
    }
    var G = [[new Float64Array(N * N), new Float64Array(N * N)], [new Float64Array(N * N), new Float64Array(N * N)]];
    var Wh = [[new Float64Array(N * N), new Float64Array(N * N)], [new Float64Array(N * N), new Float64Array(N * N)]];
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      p = i * N + j; var KX = kk(i), KY = kk(j), K2 = KX * KX + KY * KY;
      var dr = KX * U[0][0][p] + KY * U[1][0][p], di = KX * U[0][1][p] + KY * U[1][1][p];
      var s = K2 ? 1 / K2 : 0;
      G[0][0][p] = KX * dr * s; G[0][1][p] = KX * di * s; G[1][0][p] = KY * dr * s; G[1][1][p] = KY * di * s;
      for (c = 0; c < 2; c++) { Wh[c][0][p] = U[c][0][p] - G[c][0][p]; Wh[c][1][p] = U[c][1][p] - G[c][1][p]; }
    }
    function back(H) { return [dft2(H[0][0], H[0][1], true)[0], dft2(H[1][0], H[1][1], true)[0]]; }
    function deriv(H) {                                 // spectral divergence and vorticity
      var dR = new Float64Array(N * N), dI = new Float64Array(N * N), oR = new Float64Array(N * N), oI = new Float64Array(N * N);
      for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) { var p = i * N + j, KX = kk(i), KY = kk(j);
        dR[p] = -(KX * H[0][1][p] + KY * H[1][1][p]); dI[p] = KX * H[0][0][p] + KY * H[1][0][p];
        oR[p] = -(KX * H[1][1][p] - KY * H[0][1][p]); oI[p] = KX * H[1][0][p] - KY * H[0][0][p]; }
      return [dft2(dR, dI, true)[0], dft2(oR, oI, true)[0]];

    state = { u: back(U), g: back(G), w: back(Wh), du: deriv(U), dg: deriv(G), dw: deriv(Wh) };

  function maxabs(a) { var m = 0; for (var p = 0; p < a.length; p++) m = Math.max(m, Math.abs(a[p])); return m; }
  function rms(a) { var s = 0; for (var p = 0; p < a.length; p++) s += a[p] * a[p]; return Math.sqrt(s / a.length); }
  function mix(c1, c2, t) { return "rgb(" + [0, 1, 2].map(function (k) { return Math.round(c1[k] + (c2[k] - c1[k]) * t); }).join(",") + ")"; }
  function rgb(s) { var d = document.createElement("span"); d.style.color = s; document.body.appendChild(d); var c = getComputedStyle(d).color; d.remove(); return c.match(/\d+/g).slice(0, 3).map(Number); }
  function draw() {
    if (!state) return;

    var dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1, W = cv.clientWidth || 640, H = W;
    cv.width = Math.round(W * dpr); cv.height = Math.round(H * dpr);
```
