```{=html}
    var bg = rgb(css("--bg")), pos = rgb(css("--mw-pos")), neg = rgb(css("--mw-neg")), ink = css("--ink");
    var cell = W / N, m = Math.max(maxabs(state.du[0]), maxabs(state.dw[1]), 1e-300), i, j, p;
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) for (j = 0; j < N; j++) { var t = bgf[i * N + j] / m; g.fillStyle = mix(bg, t > 0 ? pos : neg, Math.min(1, Math.abs(t)) * 0.8); g.fillRect(i * cell, H - (j + 1) * cell, cell + 0.5, cell + 0.5); }
    var vm = 0; for (p = 0; p < N * N; p++) vm = Math.max(vm, Math.hypot(state.u[0][p], state.u[1][p]));
    g.strokeStyle = ink; g.fillStyle = ink; g.lineWidth = 1.2;
    for (i = 0; i < N; i++) for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      p = i * N + j; var ux = F[0][p], uy = F[1][p], mg = Math.hypot(ux, uy); if (mg < 1e-12 * vm) continue;
      var L = 1.25 * cell * mg / vm, x0 = (i + 0.5) * cell - 0.5 * L * ux / mg, y0 = H - (j + 0.5) * cell + 0.5 * L * uy / mg, x1 = x0 + L * ux / mg, y1 = y0 - L * uy / mg;
      g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x0, y0); g.lineTo(x1, y1); g.stroke();
      var a = Math.atan2(y1 - y0, x1 - x0), hl = Math.min(5, 0.4 * L);
      g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x1, y1); g.lineTo(x1 - hl * Math.cos(a - 0.5), y1 - hl * Math.sin(a - 0.5)); g.lineTo(x1 - hl * Math.cos(a + 0.5), y1 - hl * Math.sin(a + 0.5)); g.closePath(); g.fill();
    }
    var Eu = nrm2(state.u), Eg = nrm2(state.g), Ew = nrm2(state.w), cr = 0;
    for (p = 0; p < N * N; p++) cr += state.g[0][p] * state.w[0][p] + state.g[1][p] * state.w[1][p];
    cr /= N * N;
    var e = function (x) { var t = x.toExponential(1).split("e"); return t[0].replace("-", "−") + "·10<sup>" + String(parseInt(t[1], 10)).replace("-", "−") + "</sup>"; };
    var pc = function (x, d) { return x.toFixed(d); };
    out.innerHTML = "energy: ⟨|∇p|²⟩ / ⟨|u|²⟩ = " + pc(100 * Eg / Eu, 1) + "%, ⟨|ℙu|²⟩ / ⟨|u|²⟩ = " + pc(100 * Ew / Eu, 1) +
      "%, sum = " + pc(100 * (Eg + Ew) / Eu, 4) + "%<br>orthogonality: ⟨∇p · ℙu⟩ / ⟨|u|²⟩ = " + e(cr / Eu) +
      "<br>divergence (rms): u: " + e(rms(state.du[0])) + "; ℙu: " + e(rms(state.dw[0])) +
      " — vorticity (rms) of ∇p: " + e(rms(state.dg[1]));
  }
  function redo() { compute(); draw(); }
  root.querySelectorAll("input[name=wl-v]").forEach(function (b) { b.addEventListener("change", draw); });
  skc.addEventListener("input", redo);
  root.querySelector("#wl-new").addEventListener("click", function () { seed = (seed * 48271 + 11) % 2147483647; redo(); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", draw);
  new MutationObserver(draw).observe(document.documentElement, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-theme"] });
  if (window.matchMedia) { var mq = window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"); if (mq.addEventListener) mq.addEventListener("change", draw); }
  redo();
})();
</script>
```

There are thus two routes to a solenoidal field on the torus: **build** the field from a potential (Chapter 4), or **project** an arbitrary field. The following code illustrates the first route on a grid: it draws a random stream function whose energy spectrum follows a law $E(k) \propto k^{-3}$ (the law predicted by Kraichnan (1967) in the enstrophy cascade of 2D turbulence), and then derives the velocity from it by spectral differentiation.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
N, L = 256, 2 * np.pi
kv = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L / N)          # true wavenumbers
k1 = kv.copy(); k1[N // 2] = 0.0                      # for derivatives: Nyquist set to zero
KX, KY = np.meshgrid(k1, k1, indexing="ij")
kn = np.sqrt(sum(k**2 for k in np.meshgrid(kv, kv, indexing="ij")))   # true |k|
F, Fi = np.fft.fft2, lambda a: np.real(np.fft.ifft2(a))

# 1) Random stream function with target spectrum E(k) ~ k^-3 for 4 <= |k| <= 64.
#    Energy of a mode: |k|^2 |psi^_k|^2 / 2; there are about 2 pi k modes per shell.
amp = np.zeros_like(kn)
bande = (kn >= 4) & (kn <= 64)                        # also excludes the Nyquist modes (|k| >= 128)
amp[bande] = np.sqrt(kn[bande]**-3 / (np.pi * kn[bande]**3))
psi = Fi(amp * F(rng.normal(size=(N, N))))            # filtering a white noise: real psi
psi_h = F(psi)

# 2) u = (d_y psi, -d_x psi), normalized to <|u|^2> = 1
ux, uy = Fi(1j * KY * psi_h), Fi(-1j * KX * psi_h)
c = np.sqrt(np.mean(ux**2 + uy**2))
ux, uy = ux / c, uy / c

# 3) Diagnostics: divergence (recomputed from the grid), spectrum, Parseval
dxux = Fi(1j * KX * F(ux))
div = dxux + Fi(1j * KY * F(uy))
print("max|div u| =", f"{np.abs(div).max():.1e}", "; max|d_x u_x| =", f"{np.abs(dxux).max():.1f}",
      "; ratio =", f"{np.abs(div).max() / np.abs(dxux).max():.1e}")
uh2 = (np.abs(F(ux))**2 + np.abs(F(uy))**2) / N**4
E = np.array([0.5 * uh2[(kn >= s - 0.5) & (kn < s + 0.5)].sum() for s in range(N)])
s = np.arange(8, 49)
print("slope of the spectrum between k = 8 and 48 :", f"{np.polyfit(np.log(s), np.log(E[s]), 1)[0]:.2f}", "(target -3)")
print("Parseval : sum E(k) =", f"{E.sum():.12f}", "; <|u|^2>/2 =", f"{0.5 * np.mean(ux**2 + uy**2):.12f}")
# output:
# max|div u| = 8.2e-14 ; max|d_x u_x| = 12.9 ; ratio = 6.3e-15
# slope of the spectrum between k = 8 and 48 : -2.91 (target -3)
# Parseval : sum E(k) = 0.500000000000 ; <|u|^2>/2 = 0.500000000000
```

The resulting field is solenoidal to machine precision (the ratio of $6\times 10^{-15}$ reflects the rounding of FFTs on $256^2$ points) and its spectrum has the desired slope, up to statistical fluctuations: each shell contains only a few tens to a few hundreds of randomly drawn modes. Note that the amplitude is computed with the **true** wavenumbers, whereas the derivatives use the wavenumbers whose Nyquist mode is set to zero: otherwise, the Nyquist modes, whose scale equals two grid spacings, would receive the amplitude of a large-scale mode and the field would be covered by a spurious checkerboard. Building from a potential thus makes it possible to control the constraint and the spectrum at the same time; projecting makes it possible to start from any field, but modifies its spectrum.

![Velocity field built from a stream function with the previous code. Left, the level lines of $\psi$, which are the streamlines (solid lines for $\psi > 0$, dashed for $\psi < 0$), on a background colored by the vorticity $\omega = -\Delta\psi$; the vorticity is dominated by small scales, because the enstrophy spectrum $k^2E(k) \propto k^{-1}$ decays slowly. Right, the energy spectrum measured by shells, compared with the target slope $k^{-3}$.](../../../prep/p1-calcul-vectoriel/fig-courant-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="On the left, swirling level lines on a finely grained red and blue background. On the right, a scatter of points on a log-log scale that follows a straight line of slope -3 between k = 5 and k = 64."}

::: note
[Remark 6.8 — Pressure, projection method and generative models]{.tag}
For the incompressible Navier–Stokes equation, applying $\mathbb{P}$ eliminates the pressure: $\partial_t\mathbf{u} = \mathbb{P}\big[-(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{f}\big] + \nu\Delta\mathbf{u}$. The pressure is the Lagrange multiplier of the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$. Chorin's projection method (1968) first advances the velocity without pressure, then projects. Recent generative models take up this idea: Genuist et al. (2026, preprint) compare, for periodic 2D flows, six variants of a diffusion model, including several insertions of the spectral Leray projector and a simple divergence penalty; they conclude that no strategy dominates in all regimes (hard constraints win near the training distribution, the soft penalty on an out-of-distribution Taylor–Green case); Li et al. (2026, preprint) project the denoised estimate of a diffusion model of rotating 3D turbulence and obtain zero divergence to machine precision.
:::

### 6.3 With walls: why it is harder

In a periodic box, $\mathbb{P}$ is **diagonal** in Fourier space: each wave vector is treated independently of the others, in $O(1)$ operations, and the FFT does the rest. As soon as the domain has walls, several difficulties appear.

1. **A global problem.** The Neumann problem (6.1) must be solved at each projection. On a general domain, the exponentials $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$ are no longer eigenfunctions of the Laplacian with a Neumann condition: the value of $p$ at a point depends on $\mathbf{u}$ in the whole domain, and a Poisson solver is needed (multigrid, finite elements, adapted spectral methods). For a rectangle, the cosine transform still diagonalizes the problem (code below); for a cylinder, Fourier in $\theta$ is combined with a 2D problem in $(r, z)$ for each mode $m$, as in SFEMaNS.
2. **A single boundary condition.** The projection imposes $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$, but not the vanishing of the tangential velocity required by the no-slip condition of a viscous fluid. Projection methods must therefore deal with a numerical boundary layer near the walls.
3. **No more commutation.** In a bounded domain, $\mathbb{P}$ generally no longer commutes with the Laplacian or with derivatives: argument (v) of Proposition 6.6, which relied on Fourier multipliers, fails. We take this point for granted.
4. **Nonlocal magnetic conditions.** For the magnetic field, the right condition is not $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$. If the conductor is surrounded by an insulator, the outside field satisfies $\nabla\times\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$, so $\mathbf{B} = \nabla\phi$ with $\Delta\phi = 0$ outside the conductor, and it must match the inside field continuously: the boundary condition depends on the solution of an exterior problem. If the magnetic permeability $\mu$ jumps (soft-iron impellers of VKS), one must in addition match $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n}$ and the tangential component of $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{B}/\mu$ across the interface. These jump conditions are handled explicitly by SFEMaNS.
5. **The workaround by penalization.** Pseudo-spectral codes embed the cylinder and the impellers in a periodic box and impose the walls through a volume penalization term (Kreuzahler et al., 2014; in Kreuzahler et al., 2017, the periodic box measures $(3\pi)^3$ and has $384^3$ points). Projection by FFT then remains usable, at the cost of an approximate representation of the walls.

The site's literature survey (synthesis, see the [PhD proposal page](../../these/index.html#theorie)) found no generative model imposing a hard divergence constraint with the boundary conditions of a cylinder with walls; this is one of the open questions of the project.

The following code performs an exact projection (in the discrete sense) in a square closed by walls, with a MAC (*marker-and-cell*) staggered grid: the normal components of the velocity live on the cell faces, the pressure at the center. The discrete five-point Laplacian with a Neumann condition is diagonalized by the type-II cosine transform (`scipy.fft.dctn`).

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dctn, idctn
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# Box [0,1]^2 closed by walls, n x n cells of side h ("MAC" staggered grid):
#   u (x component) on the vertical faces: array (n+1, n); v on the horizontal faces: (n, n+1)
#   p and div at the cell centers: (n, n)
n = 128
h = 1.0 / n
u = rng.normal(size=(n + 1, n))
v = rng.normal(size=(n, n + 1))
u[0, :] = u[-1, :] = 0.0                # impermeability: u.n = 0 on the walls
v[:, 0] = v[:, -1] = 0.0

def divergence(u, v):
    return (u[1:, :] - u[:-1, :]) / h + (v[:, 1:] - v[:, :-1]) / h

# Discrete Poisson-Neumann problem  Lap_h p = div(u)  with  dp/dn = 0.
# The 5-point Laplacian with Neumann at the centers is diagonalized by the type-II DCT.
lam1 = (2 * np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(n) / n) - 2) / h**2
lam = lam1[:, None] + lam1[None, :]
lam[0, 0] = 1.0                          # constant mode: p defined up to a constant

d = divergence(u, v)
print("compatibility : sum of divergences * h^2 =", f"{d.sum() * h * h:.1e}")
ph = dctn(d, type=2, norm="ortho") / lam
ph[0, 0] = 0.0
p = idctn(ph, type=2, norm="ortho")

# Correction u <- u - grad_h p on the interior faces (the wall faces do not move)
u2, v2 = u.copy(), v.copy()
u2[1:-1, :] -= (p[1:, :] - p[:-1, :]) / h
v2[:, 1:-1] -= (p[:, 1:] - p[:, :-1]) / h
a, b = np.abs(d).max(), np.abs(divergence(u2, v2)).max()
print("max|div| before =", f"{a:.1e}", "; after =", f"{b:.1e}", "; ratio =", f"{b / a:.1e}")
print("u.n on the walls after projection :", np.abs(u2[[0, -1], :]).max(), np.abs(v2[:, [0, -1]]).max())
# Tangential velocity at the wall (first row of u faces near y = 0): nonzero
print("rms of the tangential velocity near the wall y = 0 :", f"{np.sqrt(np.mean(u2[:, 0]**2)):.2f}")
# output:
# compatibility : sum of divergences * h^2 = -3.6e-16
# max|div| before = 1.1e+03 ; after = 7.0e-13 ; ratio = 6.2e-16
# u.n on the walls after projection : 0.0 0.0
# rms of the tangential velocity near the wall y = 0 : 0.59
```

Three observations sum up the section. The compatibility condition of Proposition 6.2 is satisfied automatically (zero sum up to rounding) because the normal velocity vanishes on the walls. The discrete divergence is removed to machine precision, but only because the discrete gradient, divergence and Laplacian were chosen to be **compatible** on the staggered grid. Finally, the tangential velocity near the wall remains of order 1: the projection does not impose no-slip. On a non-rectangular domain, the cosine transform no longer applies and a true Poisson solver would be needed.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::
- Helmholtz–Hodge: $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w} + \nabla p$ with $\mathbf{w}$ solenoidal, a unique and orthogonal decomposition; $p$ solves a Neumann problem.
- The solenoidal part $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$ is the solenoidal field closest to $\mathbf{u}$ in the $L^2$ norm.
- On the torus, $P(\mathbf{k}) = I - \mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}^{\mathsf{T}}/|\mathbf{k}|^2$: an orthogonal projector, diagonal in Fourier space, that commutes with derivatives; the mean mode is handled separately.
- With walls, the projection is a global Poisson problem, imposes only the normal component, no longer commutes with the Laplacian, and the magnetic field requires nonlocal matching conditions.
::::

## Exercises {#exercices}

The exercises follow the order of the sessions in the work plan. One star (★) marks a direct application of the course, two stars (★★) an exercise that chains several results, three stars (★★★) a proof or a longer program, close to the questions of the internship. Work on each exercise for at least twenty minutes before reading its solution; Exercises 13 to 15 require writing and running code.

1. **★ Direct computations (session 1).** Let $f(x, y, z) = x^2 y + y z^3$ and $\mathbf{u} = (xy, \; yz, \; zx)$. (a) Compute $\nabla f$ and $\Delta f$, then check on this example that $\nabla\times(\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}$. (b) Compute $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf{u}$, then check that $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{u}) = 0$. (c) At the point $(1, 1, 1)$, compute the derivative of $f$ in the direction $\mathbf{e} = (1, 2, 2)/3$, then the largest possible rate of change of $f$ and the direction in which it is attained.

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) We find $\nabla f = (2xy, \; x^2 + z^3, \; 3yz^2)$ and $\Delta f = 2y + 0 + 6yz$. The components of the curl of $\nabla f$ are $\partial_y(3yz^2) - \partial_z(x^2 + z^3) = 3z^2 - 3z^2$, then $\partial_z(2xy) - \partial_x(3yz^2) = 0 - 0$, and finally $\partial_x(x^2 + z^3) - \partial_y(2xy) = 2x - 2x$: they all vanish.

   *(b)* We find $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = y + z + x$. The components of the curl are $\partial_y(zx) - \partial_z(yz) = -y$, then $\partial_z(xy) - \partial_x(zx) = -z$, and finally $\partial_x(yz) - \partial_y(xy) = -x$, that is

   $$
   \nabla\times\mathbf{u} = (-y, \; -z, \; -x),
   $$

   whose divergence is $\partial_x(-y) + \partial_y(-z) + \partial_z(-x) = 0$.

   *(c)* At the point $(1, 1, 1)$, $\nabla f = (2, 2, 3)$, so the directional derivative is $\nabla f\cdot\mathbf{e} = (2 + 4 + 6)/3 = 4$. By Proposition 1.6 (ii), the largest rate of change is $|\nabla f| = \sqrt{17} \approx 4.12$; it is attained in the direction $(2, 2, 3)/\sqrt{17}$, which is close to $\mathbf{e}$, hence a directional derivative of 4 that is already close to the maximum.
   :::

2. **★ The paddle wheel (session 1).** (a) For a field $\mathbf{u}$ of class $C^1$, write $J_{ij} = \partial_j u_i$ for the Jacobian matrix, $S = (J + J^{\mathsf T})/2$ for its symmetric part and $A = (J - J^{\mathsf T})/2$ for its antisymmetric part. Show that $A\mathbf{h} = \frac12\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{h}$ for every vector $\mathbf{h}$, where $\boldsymbol\omega = \nabla\times\mathbf{u}$, and deduce that the motion in the neighborhood of a point is the sum of a translation, a pure strain and a solid-body rotation with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega/2$. (b) Apply this result to the shear $\mathbf{u} = (y, 0, 0)$: in which direction and at what speed does a small paddle wheel with axis $\mathbf{e}_z$ rotate? Give a physical explanation. (c) What does the same wheel do in the point vortex $\mathbf{u} = \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi r}\mathbf{e}_\theta$ of Example 1.16?

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) With $\omega_j = \varepsilon_{jlm}\partial_l u_m$ and the cyclic permutation $\varepsilon_{ijk} = \varepsilon_{jki}$:

   $$
   \tfrac12(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{h})_i = \tfrac12\varepsilon_{ijk}\,\omega_j\,h_k = \tfrac12\varepsilon_{jki}\varepsilon_{jlm}\,\partial_l u_m\,h_k.
   $$

   Lemma 1.12 gives $\varepsilon_{jki}\varepsilon_{jlm} = \delta_{kl}\delta_{im} - \delta_{km}\delta_{il}$, hence

   $$
   \tfrac12(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{h})_i = \tfrac12(\delta_{kl}\delta_{im} - \delta_{km}\delta_{il})\,\partial_l u_m\,h_k = \tfrac12(\partial_k u_i - \partial_i u_k)\,h_k,
   $$

   which is exactly $(A\mathbf{h})_i$. The Taylor expansion therefore reads $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{h}) = \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) + S\mathbf{h} + \frac12\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{h} + o(|\mathbf{h}|)$. The first term is a translation. The matrix $S$ is real symmetric, hence diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis: $S\mathbf{h}$ stretches or compresses the neighborhood along three perpendicular axes, without rotating it. The last term is the velocity field of a solid-body rotation with angular velocity vector $\boldsymbol\omega/2$ (Proposition 1.8 (ii)).

   *(b)* For $\mathbf{u} = (y, 0, 0)$, only $J_{12} = \partial_y u_x = 1$ is nonzero, and $\boldsymbol\omega = (0, 0, -1)$. The wheel therefore rotates clockwise with angular velocity $1/2$. Physically, the upper blades are dragged to the right faster than the lower ones: the torque makes the wheel turn. The symmetric part $S$, with eigenvalues $\pm 1/2$ and eigendirections $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$, stretches the neighborhood along the first diagonal and compresses it along the second: shear is the sum of a pure strain and a rotation.

   *(c)* For $r > 0$, the vorticity of the point vortex vanishes: the wheel travels around a circle about the axis, but keeps a fixed orientation, like a Ferris wheel gondola. The blades close to the axis are faster than the outer blades, which would tend to make the wheel turn one way, but the curvature of the trajectory exactly compensates this effect.
   :::

3. **★★ Cylindrical coordinates (session 2).** (a) The Rankine vortex is defined by $u_r = u_z = 0$ and $u_\theta = \Omega r$ for $r \le a$, $u_\theta = \Omega a^2/r$ for $r > a$. Compute its vorticity in both regions and its circulation on a circle of radius $R > a$ centered on the axis, then check Stokes' theorem. (b) The uniform field $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{e}_x$ reads $u_r = \cos\theta$, $u_\theta = -\sin\theta$, $u_z = 0$. Check with (1.2) that its divergence vanishes, then with (1.5) that its vector Laplacian vanishes. What would the “component-by-component” Laplacian $(\Delta u_r, \Delta u_\theta)$ give? Conclude.

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) By (1.3), $\omega_z = \frac1r\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}(r u_\theta)$. Inside, $\omega_z = \frac1r\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}(\Omega r^2) = 2\Omega$: the core rotates as a solid body. Outside, $r u_\theta = \Omega a^2$ is constant and $\omega_z = 0$. The circulation on the circle of radius $R > a$ is $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\Omega a^2}{R}\,R\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi\Omega a^2$. The flux of the vorticity through the corresponding disk is $2\Omega\times\pi a^2$, since the vorticity is concentrated in the core: the two sides of (3.2) coincide. The circulation does not depend on $R$; seen from afar, the Rankine vortex is a point vortex with circulation $\Gamma = 2\pi\Omega a^2$.

   *(b)* By (1.2), $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = \frac1r\partial_r(r\cos\theta) + \frac1r\partial_\theta(-\sin\theta) = \frac{\cos\theta}{r} - \frac{\cos\theta}{r} = 0$. By (1.4), $\Delta u_r = \frac{1}{r^2}\partial_\theta^2\cos\theta = -\frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}$ and $\Delta u_\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{r^2}$. Formula (1.5) then gives

   $$
   (\Delta\mathbf{u})_r = -\frac{\cos\theta}{r^2} - \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2} - \frac{2}{r^2}\,\partial_\theta(-\sin\theta) = 0,
   $$

   and, likewise,

   $$
   (\Delta\mathbf{u})_\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{r^2} + \frac{\sin\theta}{r^2} + \frac{2}{r^2}\,\partial_\theta(\cos\theta) = 0.
   $$

   The component-by-component Laplacian would give $(-\cos\theta, \sin\theta)/r^2$, which is not zero: it would attribute a “curvature” to a constant field. The extra terms of (1.5) correct for the effect of the rotation of the basis vectors; forgetting them is a common mistake in codes written in cylindrical coordinates.
   :::

4. **★★ Product rules (session 3).** Prove formulas (a), (c) and (f) of Proposition 2.5. For (f), one may start by establishing $[\mathbf{u}\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{v})]_i = u_j\,\partial_i v_j - u_j\,\partial_j v_i$.

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) By the Leibniz rule, $\partial_i(fg) = f\,\partial_i g + g\,\partial_i f$.

   *(c)* $[\nabla\times(f\mathbf{u})]_i = \varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_j(f u_k) = f\,\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_j u_k + \varepsilon_{ijk}(\partial_j f)\,u_k = f\,(\nabla\times\mathbf{u})_i + (\nabla f\times\mathbf{u})_i$.

   (f) By Lemma 1.12, with $\varepsilon_{ijk} = \varepsilon_{kij}$:

   $$
   [\mathbf{u}\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{v})]_i = \varepsilon_{ijk}\,u_j\,\varepsilon_{klm}\partial_l v_m = (\delta_{il}\delta_{jm} - \delta_{im}\delta_{jl})\,u_j\,\partial_l v_m = u_j\,\partial_i v_j - u_j\,\partial_j v_i.
   $$

   Hence $u_j\partial_i v_j = [\mathbf{u}\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{v})]_i + [(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}]_i$ and, exchanging the roles, $v_j\partial_i u_j = [\mathbf{v}\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{u})]_i + [(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}]_i$. The sum of the two is $\partial_i(u_j v_j) = [\nabla(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})]_i$, which is (f).
   :::

5. **★★ The ABC flow, an exact solution (session 3).** Let $\mathbf{u}$ be the ABC flow of Example 1.10. (a) Using the Lamb form (2.2), show that $(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = \nabla(|\mathbf{u}|^2/2)$. (b) Deduce that $\mathbf{u}$ is a steady solution of the incompressible Euler equations $\partial_t\mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = -\nabla p$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$, and give the pressure. (c) Now take this field as a magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Show that the Lorentz force $\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B}$ vanishes and interpret this result with (2.3). (d) In a conductor at rest, what becomes of this magnetic field under the induction equation (2.4)?

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) Since $\boldsymbol\omega = \mathbf{u}$, we have $\mathbf{u}\times\boldsymbol\omega = \mathbf{0}$ and (2.2) reduces to $(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = \nabla(|\mathbf{u}|^2/2)$.

   *(b)* With $p = -|\mathbf{u}|^2/2 + \text{const}$, we have $(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = -\nabla p$; the time-independent field therefore satisfies the Euler equation, and it is divergence-free. It is an exact steady solution, whose streamlines can be chaotic (Dombre et al., 1986).

   *(c)* We have $\mathbf{j} = \nabla\times\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B}$, so $\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$: the field is said to be **force-free**. By (2.3), the magnetic tension $(\mathbf{B}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{B}$ exactly balances the magnetic pressure gradient $\nabla(|\mathbf{B}|^2/2)$ there.

   *(d)* With $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$, (2.4) reduces to $\partial_t\mathbf{B} = \eta\Delta\mathbf{B} = -\eta\mathbf{B}$ (Example 2.8), hence $\mathbf{B}(t) = e^{-\eta t}\mathbf{B}(0)$: the field decays exponentially through Ohmic dissipation. For it to grow, a flow is needed that can stretch the field lines faster than diffusion dissipates them; experiment E3 of the repository measures the growth rate obtained when the flow is itself the ABC flow, as a function of $Rm$ (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e3)).
   :::

6. **★ The Coulomb field (session 4).** Let $\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}/|\mathbf{x}|^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$. (a) Show that $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0$ away from the origin. (b) Compute the outward flux of $\mathbf{E}$ through the sphere of radius $R$ centered at $\mathbf{0}$. (c) Show that this flux is zero through every sphere that does not enclose the origin, and that it equals $4\pi$ through every smooth closed surface that encloses it. (d) Why is there no contradiction with Proposition 3.8? What would it take for a magnetic field to behave like this?

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) With $r = |\mathbf{x}|$ and $\partial_i r = x_i/r$: $\partial_i(x_i r^{-3}) = 3r^{-3} + x_i\cdot(-3)r^{-4}\cdot\frac{x_i}{r} = 3r^{-3} - 3r^{-3} = 0$.

   *(b)* On the sphere, $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{x}/R$ and $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 1/R^2$; the flux equals $\frac{1}{R^2}\times 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi$, whatever $R$.

   *(c)* If the sphere does not enclose the origin, $\mathbf{E}$ is of class $C^1$ on the ball it bounds and Theorem 3.5 gives a flux equal to $\int\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0$. If a closed surface $S$ encloses the origin, we choose a small sphere $S_\varepsilon$ centered at $\mathbf{0}$ and lying inside $S$. The domain between the two does not contain the origin; its boundary consists of $S$ (outward normal) and $S_\varepsilon$ (normal pointing toward the origin). Theorem 3.5 gives $\Phi(S) - \Phi(S_\varepsilon) = 0$ there, hence $\Phi(S) = 4\pi$.

   *(d)* Proposition 3.8 assumes the field to be of class $C^1$ on the whole open set; here $\mathbf{E}$ is not defined at $\mathbf{0}$, and all the flux comes from this singular point: it is the field of a point charge (in the sense of distributions, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 4\pi\delta_{\mathbf{0}}$). For a magnetic field, a point “magnetic charge”, that is a monopole, would be needed, and none has ever been observed. The code block of Chapter 3 and the figure of Section 3.3 illustrate these two cases.
   :::

7. **★★ Green and Ampère (session 4).** (a) With $P = -y/2$ and $Q = x/2$ in Theorem 3.4, show that the area of a planar domain $D$ equals $\frac12\oint_{\partial D}(x\,\mathrm{d}y - y\,\mathrm{d}x)$, and deduce the area of the ellipse with semi-axes $a$ and $b$. (b) An infinite cylindrical wire of radius $a$ and axis $\mathbf{e}_z$ carries a current $I$ of uniform density $\mathbf{j} = \frac{I}{\pi a^2}\mathbf{e}_z$. Assuming that $\mathbf{B} = B_\theta(r)\,\mathbf{e}_\theta$, compute $B_\theta$ inside and outside the wire using Stokes' theorem applied to $\nabla\times\mathbf{B} = \mu_0\mathbf{j}$. Check the result with (1.2) and (1.3).

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) We have $\partial_x Q - \partial_y P = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1$, so the right-hand side of Theorem 3.4 is the area of $D$. For the ellipse $x = a\cos t$, $y = b\sin t$, we have $x\,\mathrm{d}y - y\,\mathrm{d}x = (ab\cos^2 t + ab\sin^2 t)\,\mathrm{d}t = ab\,\mathrm{d}t$, and the area equals $\frac12\times 2\pi ab = \pi ab$.

   *(b)* On a circle of radius $r$ centered on the axis, $\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\ell = 2\pi r\,B_\theta(r)$. The flux of $\mu_0\mathbf{j}$ through the corresponding disk is $\mu_0 I r^2/a^2$ if $r \le a$ and $\mu_0 I$ if $r \ge a$. Hence

   $$
   B_\theta(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I\,r}{2\pi a^2} \quad (r \le a), \qquad B_\theta(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \quad (r \ge a),
   $$

   two expressions that match at $r = a$. Check: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = \frac1r\partial_\theta B_\theta = 0$, and $(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})_z = \frac1r\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}(rB_\theta)$ equals $\frac1r\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}\big(\frac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\pi a^2}\big) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi a^2} = \mu_0 j$ inside and $0$ outside. The singular field of Example 3.9 is the limit $a \to 0$, where the whole current density is concentrated on the axis.
   :::

8. **★★ Kinetic energy budget (session 4).** In a periodic box, consider a smooth solution of the Navier–Stokes equations $\partial_t\mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = -\nabla p + \nu\Delta\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{f}$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$. Show that (a) $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla p\rangle = 0$; (b) $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u}\rangle = 0$; (c) $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{u}\rangle = -\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle$. Deduce the budget

   $$
   \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Big\langle\frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2}\Big\rangle = \langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle - \nu\,\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle,
   $$

   interpret each term, and say where the assumption $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ is used.

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) By (3.3) without boundary term, $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla p\rangle = -\langle p\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}\rangle = 0$.

   *(b)* We have $u_i u_j\partial_j u_i = u_j\,\partial_j(|\mathbf{u}|^2/2) = \nabla\cdot\big(\mathbf{u}\,|\mathbf{u}|^2/2\big) - \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2}\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}$. The average of the divergence of a periodic field is zero (Theorem 3.5 on the box, the fluxes through opposite faces cancelling each other), and the second term vanishes by incompressibility.

   *(c)* Theorem 2.3 with $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0$ gives $\Delta\mathbf{u} = -\nabla\times\boldsymbol\omega$, then (3.4) without boundary term gives $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\times\boldsymbol\omega\rangle = \langle\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\nabla\times\mathbf{u}\rangle = \langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle$.

   Multiplying the equation by $\mathbf{u}$ and averaging gives the stated budget. The term $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle$ is the power injected by the forcing; $\nu\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle \ge 0$ is the viscous dissipation. Advection and pressure neither create nor destroy energy: they redistribute it in space and among scales (this is the cascade of the module [Fluid mechanics and turbulence](../p2-mecanique-fluides/index.html)). Incompressibility is used in all three points. In MHD, the Lorentz force $\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B}$ is added to the right-hand side: the kinetic budget gains the term $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B})\rangle$, which is exactly the opposite of the exchange term of Proposition 3.10. The total energy therefore satisfies $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E = \langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle - \nu\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle - \eta\langle|\mathbf{j}|^2\rangle$.
   :::

9. **★★ Stream function (session 5).** Let $\psi = \sin x\sin y$ on the torus $[0, 2\pi)^2$ and $\mathbf{u} = \nabla^\perp\psi$ (Example 4.6). (a) Compute the flow rate of $\mathbf{u}$ through the segment going from $(0, 0)$ to $(\pi/2, \pi/2)$ in two ways: with Proposition 4.5 (iv), then by a direct computation. (b) Show more generally that, if the vorticity is a function of the stream function, $\omega = F(\psi)$, the flow is a steady solution of the 2D Euler equation written in vorticity form, $\partial_t\omega + \mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\omega = 0$. Apply this to $\psi = \sin x\sin y$. (c) Can a uniform flow $\mathbf{u} = U\mathbf{e}_x$ be written $\nabla^\perp\psi$ with a periodic $\psi$? What must be added to the stream-function representation on the torus?

   ::: sol
   *Solution.* (a) By Proposition 4.5 (iv), the flow rate equals $\psi(\pi/2, \pi/2) - \psi(0, 0) = 1$. Directly: the segment is parametrized by $\boldsymbol\gamma(s) = (s, s)$, $s \in [0, \pi/2]$, the unnormalized normal is $(\gamma_y', -\gamma_x') = (1, -1)$ and $\mathbf{u}(\boldsymbol\gamma(s)) = (\sin s\cos s, \; -\cos s\sin s)$. We therefore have $\mathbf{u}\cdot(1, -1) = 2\sin s\cos s = \sin 2s$, whose integral over $[0, \pi/2]$ equals 1.

   *(b)* By the chain rule, $\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\omega = F'(\psi)\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\psi = 0$ by Proposition 4.5 (iii). The time-independent field $\omega$ therefore satisfies $\partial_t\omega + \mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\omega = 0$. For $\psi = \sin x\sin y$, $\omega = 2\psi$: the function $F$ is linear.

   *(c)* The function $\psi = Uy$ does give $\mathbf{u} = (U, 0)$, but it is not periodic in $y$. More generally, for periodic $\psi$, $\langle\nabla^\perp\psi\rangle = \mathbf{0}$, because the average of a derivative of a periodic function is zero. On the torus, a divergence-free field is therefore written $\bar{\mathbf{u}} + \nabla^\perp\psi$: two constants for the mean field, plus a periodic stream function (Remark 4.3 and Theorem 6.4). A generative model that produces only $\psi$ cannot represent a nonzero mean field: it must be generated separately, or one must check that it vanishes in the data.
   :::

10. **★★★ Poincaré lemma for solenoidal fields (session 5).** Let $\Omega$ be a domain that is star-shaped with respect to the origin and $\mathbf{B}$ a field of class $C^1$ on $\Omega$ such that $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$. Set $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_0^1 t\,\mathbf{B}(t\mathbf{x})\times\mathbf{x}\,\mathrm{d}t$. (a) Show that $\nabla\times\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$ (Theorem 4.2 (ii)). (b) Compute $\mathbf{A}$ for $\mathbf{B} = B_0\mathbf{e}_z$ and compare with Example 4.9. (c) Show that $\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$ and that $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = \int_0^1 t^2\,\mathbf{x}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})(t\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}t$. Is this potential in the Coulomb gauge in general?

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* (a) We write $A_m = \int_0^1 t\,\varepsilon_{mjk}B_j(t\mathbf{x})\,x_k\,\mathrm{d}t$ and differentiate under the integral sign, noting that $\partial_l[B_j(t\mathbf{x})] = t\,(\partial_l B_j)(t\mathbf{x})$. With $\varepsilon_{ilm}\varepsilon_{mjk} = \varepsilon_{mil}\varepsilon_{mjk} = \delta_{ij}\delta_{lk} - \delta_{ik}\delta_{lj}$ (Lemma 1.12):

    $$
    (\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_i = \int_0^1 t\,\varepsilon_{ilm}\varepsilon_{mjk}\,\partial_l\big[B_j(t\mathbf{x})\,x_k\big]\,\mathrm{d}t,
    $$

    with

    $$
    \partial_l\big[B_j(t\mathbf{x})\,x_k\big] = t\,x_k(\partial_l B_j)(t\mathbf{x}) + B_j(t\mathbf{x})\,\delta_{lk}.
    $$

    The first product of symbols gives $t\,x_l(\partial_l B_i)(t\mathbf{x}) + 3B_i(t\mathbf{x})$, the second $-t\,x_i(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B})(t\mathbf{x}) - B_i(t\mathbf{x})$, whose first part vanishes since $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$. The integrand is therefore

    $$
    t^2\,x_l(\partial_l B_i)(t\mathbf{x}) + 2t\,B_i(t\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big[t^2 B_i(t\mathbf{x})\big],
    $$

    whose integral between 0 and 1 equals $B_i(\mathbf{x})$. Star-shapedness guarantees that $t\mathbf{x} \in \Omega$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.

    *(b)* For $\mathbf{B} = B_0\mathbf{e}_z$, $\mathbf{A} = \big(\int_0^1 t\,\mathrm{d}t\big)B_0\,\mathbf{e}_z\times\mathbf{x} = \frac{B_0}{2}(-y, x, 0)$: this is the symmetric potential of Example 4.9.

    *(c)* $\mathbf{x}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{x}) = 0$ for every $t$, hence $\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$. For the divergence, $\partial_i A_i = \int_0^1 t\,\varepsilon_{ijk}\big[t\,x_k(\partial_i B_j)(t\mathbf{x}) + B_j(t\mathbf{x})\,\delta_{ik}\big]\,\mathrm{d}t$; the second term contains $\varepsilon_{iji} = 0$, and the first equals $t^2 x_k\varepsilon_{kij}\partial_i B_j = t^2\,\mathbf{x}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})$. This is not zero in general: for $\mathbf{B} = (0, 0, x)$, which is divergence-free, $\nabla\times\mathbf{B} = (0, -1, 0)$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = -y/3$. This potential satisfies the condition $\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$ (sometimes called the Poincaré gauge); to switch to the Coulomb gauge, one solves the Poisson equation of Proposition 4.8.
    :::

11. **★ Fourier series of the triangle wave (session 6).** Let $f$ be the $2\pi$-periodic function equal to $|x|$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$. (a) Compute its Fourier coefficients. How do they decay, and why faster than those of the square wave of Example 5.6? (b) By evaluating the series at $x = 0$, show that $\sum_{n\ \text{odd}\ \ge 1}1/n^2 = \pi^2/8$. (c) Using Parseval's identity, show that $\sum_{n\ \text{odd}\ \ge 1}1/n^4 = \pi^4/96$, and then that $\sum_{n \ge 1}1/n^4 = \pi^4/90$.

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* (a) We have $\hat f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|x|\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and, by parity and then integration by parts,

    $$
    \hat f_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x\cos(nx)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{\pi}\Big[\frac{x\sin(nx)}{n} + \frac{\cos(nx)}{n^2}\Big]_0^\pi = \frac{(-1)^n - 1}{\pi n^2},
    $$

    that is $-\frac{2}{\pi n^2}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for nonzero even $n$. The coefficients decay like $1/n^2$: $f$ is continuous and its derivative is the square wave $\operatorname{sign}(\sin x)$ of Example 5.6. Proposition 5.4 gives $\hat f_n = \widehat{(f')}_n/(in) = \frac{2}{i\pi n}\cdot\frac{1}{in} = -\frac{2}{\pi n^2}$, which confirms the computation: one more integration, one more factor $1/n$.

    *(b)* The function $f$ is continuous and piecewise $C^1$; by Theorem 5.3 (ii), its series converges uniformly: $f(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n\ \text{odd}\ \ge 1}\frac{\cos(nx)}{n^2}$. At $x = 0$, we obtain $0 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{\text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^2}$, hence the result.

    *(c)* The left-hand side of (5.1) equals $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\pi^2}{3}$. The right-hand side equals $\frac{\pi^2}{4} + 2\sum_{\text{odd}}\frac{4}{\pi^2 n^4}$. We deduce $\sum_{\text{odd}}\frac{1}{n^4} = \frac{\pi^2}{8}\Big(\frac{\pi^2}{3} - \frac{\pi^2}{4}\Big) = \frac{\pi^4}{96}$. Finally, writing $S = \sum_{n\ge1}1/n^4$, the sum over even integers equals $S/16$, so $S - S/16 = \pi^4/96$ and $S = \pi^4/90$.
    :::

12. **★★ Aliasing and the 2/3 rule (session 6).** (a) On a grid of $N = 16$ points of $[0, 2\pi)$, to which functions of wavenumber at most 8 are the functions $\sin(21x)$, $\cos(12x)$ and $\sin(8x)$ indistinguishable? Check with the interactive diagram of Section 5.2. (b) A pseudo-spectral code keeps the modes $|n| \le K = 21$ and computes quadratic terms. What is the smallest $N$ that eliminates aliasing on these modes? (c) For a cubic term $u^3$, show that $N \ge 4K + 1$ is needed, that is, only half of the spectrum can be kept.

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* (a) Since $21 = 16 + 5$, $\sin(21x)$ coincides on the grid with $\sin(5x)$. Since $12 = 16 - 4$, $\cos(12x_j) = \cos(-4x_j) = \cos(4x_j)$. Finally, $\sin(8x_j) = \sin(\pi j) = 0$: the Nyquist mode in sine is invisible on the grid, which also justifies the convention of Definition 5.11.

    *(b)* By Theorem 5.16, $N \ge 3K + 1 = 64$ is needed. This is the usual choice: $64$ points to keep the modes $|n| \le 21$, that is, one third of $64$.

    *(c)* The product $u^3$ has modes up to $3K$. By (5.2), the discrete coefficient of index $n$, $|n| \le K$, receives the folded terms $\widehat{(u^3)}_{n + pN}$, $p \neq 0$, with $|n + pN| \ge N - K$. They all vanish if $N - K > 3K$, that is $N \ge 4K + 1$. Only the modes $|n| \le N/4$ are then kept, half of the representable spectrum.
    :::

13. **★★ Smoothness and rate of convergence (code, session 6).** Using Propositions 5.4 and 5.12, predict the rate of convergence of the spectral derivative of $f(x) = |\sin x|^3$. Check numerically by comparing with $e^{\sin x}$.

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* Near $x = 0$, $f(x) \approx |x|^3$, whose successive derivatives are $3x|x|$, $6|x|$ and $6\operatorname{sign}(x)$: $f$ is of class $C^2$ and its third derivative is piecewise continuous with jumps at $0$ and at $\pi$. Three integrations by parts give $\hat f_n = \widehat{(f''')}_n/(in)^3$ and, as for the square wave, $\widehat{(f''')}_n = O(1/n)$; hence $|\hat f_n| = O(n^{-4})$. Proposition 5.12 with $q = 4$ predicts an error in $O(N^{-2})$: it should be divided by 4 when $N$ doubles. For $e^{\sin x}$, an analytic function, the convergence is exponential.

    ```python
    import numpy as np

    def derivee_spectrale(f):
        N = f.size
        k = np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=1 / N)            # integer wavenumbers (L = 2 pi)
        if N % 2 == 0:
            k[N // 2] = 0.0
        return np.real(np.fft.ifft(1j * k * np.fft.fft(f)))

    print("   N   error e^(sin x)    error |sin x|^3    ratio")
    e_prec = None
    for N in [16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
        x = 2 * np.pi * np.arange(N) / N
        e1 = np.abs(derivee_spectrale(np.exp(np.sin(x))) - np.cos(x) * np.exp(np.sin(x))).max()
        e2 = np.abs(derivee_spectrale(np.abs(np.sin(x))**3)
                    - 3 * np.abs(np.sin(x)) * np.sin(x) * np.cos(x)).max()
        r = "  -" if e_prec is None else f"{e_prec / e2:.2f}"
        print(f"{N:4d}   {e1:.1e}            {e2:.1e}            {r}")
        e_prec = e2
    # output:
    #    N   error e^(sin x)    error |sin x|^3    ratio
    #   16   1.8e-07            1.7e-02              -
    #   32   2.9e-15            4.4e-03            3.93
    #   64   1.1e-14            1.1e-03            3.98
    #  128   2.4e-14            2.7e-04            4.00
    #  256   5.5e-14            6.8e-05            4.00
    #  512   1.2e-13            1.7e-05            4.00
    ```

    The ratio of successive errors tends to 4, as predicted, whereas $e^{\sin x}$ reaches machine precision as early as $N = 32$. The spectral method is therefore not “magic”: it is as accurate as the function is smooth. This is why pseudo-spectral codes that represent objects with sharp edges, such as the VKS impellers, must filter the discontinuities (Remark 5.17).
    :::

14. **★★★ Leray projection in 2D through the stream function (code, session 7).** (a) On the 2D torus, show in Fourier space that $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u} = \langle\mathbf{u}\rangle + \nabla^\perp\psi$, where $\psi$ is the zero-mean solution of $-\Delta\psi = \omega$ and $\omega = \partial_x u_y - \partial_y u_x$. (b) Deduce that $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbb{P}\mathbf{u}$ have the same vorticity, and interpret. (c) Program both computations on a random field and check that they coincide up to rounding.

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* (a) For $\mathbf{k} \neq \mathbf{0}$, $\hat\omega = i(k_x\hat u_y - k_y\hat u_x)$, $\hat\psi = \hat\omega/|\mathbf{k}|^2$ and $\widehat{\nabla^\perp\psi} = (ik_y\hat\psi, \; -ik_x\hat\psi)$. The first component equals

    $$
    \frac{ik_y\cdot i(k_x\hat u_y - k_y\hat u_x)}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} = \frac{k_y^2\hat u_x - k_x k_y\hat u_y}{|\mathbf{k}|^2} = \hat u_x - \frac{k_x(k_x\hat u_x + k_y\hat u_y)}{|\mathbf{k}|^2},
    $$

    using $k_y^2 = |\mathbf{k}|^2 - k_x^2$. This is the first component of (6.2); the second is handled likewise. The mode $\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$ gives the mean field, which $\mathbb{P}$ preserves.

    *(b)* The vorticity of $\nabla^\perp\psi$ equals $-\Delta\psi = \omega$ (Proposition 4.5 (ii)) and the mean field has none. The projection removes the gradient part, which has no vorticity ($\nabla\times\nabla p = \mathbf{0}$): it modifies the divergence and leaves the vorticity intact. In 2D, projecting therefore amounts to “reconstructing the velocity from its vorticity”.

    *(c)* We first remove the Nyquist modes, whose derivative is not defined (Remark 6.7); without this precaution, the two computations differ on these few modes.

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
    N = 128
    k1 = np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=1 / N); k1[N // 2] = 0.0      # integer wavenumbers, Nyquist set to zero
    KX, KY = np.meshgrid(k1, k1, indexing="ij")
    K2 = KX**2 + KY**2
    K2s = np.where(K2 == 0, 1.0, K2)
    F, Fi = np.fft.fft2, lambda a: np.real(np.fft.ifft2(a))

    u = rng.normal(size=(2, N, N)) + np.array([0.3, -0.2])[:, None, None]   # noise + mean field
    uh = np.stack([F(u[0]), F(u[1])])
    nyq = np.zeros((N, N), bool); nyq[N // 2, :] = nyq[:, N // 2] = True
    uh[:, nyq] = 0.0                                        # Nyquist modes removed (derivative not defined)
    u = np.stack([Fi(uh[0]), Fi(uh[1])])

    # (a) Leray: u^ - k (k . u^)/|k|^2  (the mode k = 0 is kept)
    kd = KX * uh[0] + KY * uh[1]
    P1 = np.stack([Fi(uh[0] - KX * kd / K2s), Fi(uh[1] - KY * kd / K2s)])

    # (b) Stream function: omega = d_x u_y - d_y u_x, -Lap psi = omega, Pu = <u> + (d_y psi, -d_x psi)
    om_h = 1j * KX * uh[1] - 1j * KY * uh[0]
    psi_h = om_h / K2s
    psi_h[0, 0] = 0.0
    P2 = np.stack([Fi(1j * KY * psi_h), Fi(-1j * KX * psi_h)]) + u.mean(axis=(1, 2))[:, None, None]

    div = Fi(1j * KX * F(P2[0]) + 1j * KY * F(P2[1]))
    print("max|P1 - P2| =", f"{np.abs(P1 - P2).max():.1e}", "; max|div P2| =", f"{np.abs(div).max():.1e}")
    print("mean preserved :", np.round(P2.mean(axis=(1, 2)), 12), "; vorticity unchanged :",
          f"{np.abs(Fi(1j * KX * F(P2[1]) - 1j * KY * F(P2[0])) - Fi(om_h)).max():.1e}")
    # output:
    # max|P1 - P2| = 8.9e-16 ; max|div P2| = 3.9e-14
    # mean preserved : [ 0.31141623 -0.20974851] ; vorticity unchanged : 8.5e-14
    ```

    The two computations agree to within $10^{-15}$, the divergence of the result is at the level of FFT rounding, the mean field is preserved and the vorticity has not changed.
    :::

15. **★★★ Vector potential and magnetic helicity (code, session 7).** (a) In Fourier space, show that $H_M = \langle\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}\overline{\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ does not change when $\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}}$ is replaced by $\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathbf{k}} + i\mathbf{k}\hat\chi_{\mathbf{k}}$: this is a second proof of Proposition 4.10. (b) Program: draw a smooth, solenoidal, zero-mean field $\mathbf{B}$ on the 3D torus; compute its potential in the Coulomb gauge with Proposition 4.8; check $\nabla\times\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A} = 0$; compare $H_M$ in two gauges. (c) Test the program on the ABC field, for which $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$ and $H_M = A^2 + B^2 + C^2$ (Example 4.9). (d) Why was $\mathbf{B}$ required to have zero mean?

    ::: sol
    *Solution.* (a) The variation of $H_M$ equals $\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\overline{i\mathbf{k}\hat\chi_{\mathbf{k}}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \sum_{\mathbf{k}}(-i)\,\overline{\hat\chi_{\mathbf{k}}}\,(\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}) = 0$, since $\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = 0$ for a solenoidal field. Each Fourier mode is separately gauge invariant.

    *(b)* and (c):

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
    N, L = 32, 2 * np.pi
    kv = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L / N)            # true wavenumbers
    filtre = np.exp(-sum(k**2 for k in np.meshgrid(kv, kv, kv, indexing="ij")) / 8)
    k1 = kv.copy(); k1[N // 2] = 0.0                       # Nyquist set to zero for derivatives
    K = np.stack(np.meshgrid(k1, k1, k1, indexing="ij"))
    K2 = (K**2).sum(0)
    K2s = np.where(K2 == 0, 1.0, K2)
    F  = lambda a: np.fft.fftn(a, axes=(-3, -2, -1))
    Fi = lambda a: np.real(np.fft.ifftn(a, axes=(-3, -2, -1)))
    croix = lambda a, b: np.stack([a[1]*b[2] - a[2]*b[1], a[2]*b[0] - a[0]*b[2], a[0]*b[1] - a[1]*b[0]])

    # Smooth random B, divergence-free and with zero mean (Leray projection)
    Bh = F(rng.normal(size=(3, N, N, N))) * filtre
    Bh = Bh - K * (K * Bh).sum(0) / K2s
    Bh[:, 0, 0, 0] = 0.0
    Bh = Bh / np.sqrt(np.mean((Fi(Bh)**2).sum(0)))         # normalization <|B|^2> = 1
    B = Fi(Bh)

    # Vector potential in the Coulomb gauge: -Lap A = rot B  =>  A^ = i k x B^ / |k|^2
    Ah = 1j * croix(K, Bh) / K2s
    A = Fi(Ah)
    print("max|rot A - B| =", f"{np.abs(Fi(1j * croix(K, Ah)) - B).max():.1e}",
          "; max|div A| =", f"{np.abs(Fi((1j * K * Ah).sum(0))).max():.1e}", "; max|B| =", f"{np.abs(B).max():.1f}")
    HM = np.mean((A * B).sum(0))
    chi = Fi(F(rng.normal(size=(N, N, N))) * filtre)
    A2 = A + Fi(1j * K * F(chi))                           # another gauge, same B
    print("H_M (Coulomb) =", f"{HM:.12f}", "; H_M (A + grad chi) =", f"{np.mean((A2 * B).sum(0)):.12f}")

    # Analytical check: for the ABC field (Beltrami field k = 1), A = B in the Coulomb gauge, H_M = A^2 + B^2 + C^2
    x = L * np.arange(N) / N
    X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(x, x, x, indexing="ij")
    a, b, c = 1.0, 0.8, 0.6
    Babc = np.stack([a*np.sin(Z) + c*np.cos(Y), b*np.sin(X) + a*np.cos(Z), c*np.sin(Y) + b*np.cos(X)])
    Aabc = Fi(1j * croix(K, F(Babc)) / K2s)
    print("ABC : max|A - B| =", f"{np.abs(Aabc - Babc).max():.1e}", "; H_M =", f"{np.mean((Aabc * Babc).sum(0)):.12f}")
    # output:
    # max|rot A - B| = 5.6e-15 ; max|div A| = 8.2e-17 ; max|B| = 2.2
    # H_M (Coulomb) = -0.039622643548 ; H_M (A + grad chi) = -0.039622643548
    # ABC : max|A - B| = 8.9e-16 ; H_M = 2.000000000000
    ```

    The potential reproduces $\mathbf{B}$ to within $10^{-15}$, it is indeed in the Coulomb gauge, and the helicity is identical in both gauges up to the twelfth decimal place. On the ABC field, the program recovers $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$ and $H_M = 1 + 0.64 + 0.36 = 2$.

    *(d)* A mean field $\bar{\mathbf{B}} \neq \mathbf{0}$ has no periodic potential (Remark 4.3): $\bar{\mathbf{B}} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}$ requires an $\mathbf{A}$ that grows linearly, as in Example 4.9, and $\langle\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle$ is then no longer defined on the torus. This is why the formula of Proposition 4.8 excludes the mode $\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}$. With walls, an analogous difficulty forces the use of a “relative” helicity when $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} \neq 0$ on the boundary (Berger and Field, 1984).
    :::

## Connection with the internship {#lien-stage}

The [internship offer](https://scheng2024.github.io/stage_milady_2027.pdf) asks for conditional generative models of parameter-dependent physical fields to be built, for constraints derived from the PDEs and boundary conditions to be imposed on them “through model design, training losses, or sampling procedures”, and for them to be validated with metrics on “energy spectra, helicity, divergence control, and topology preservation”. Each of these terms points to a chapter of this module.

**Zero divergence: build or project.** The five constraint mechanisms compared in experiment E2 of the repository, devoted to the conditional generation (on the diffusivity $\eta$) of forced 2D MHD fields, all come under this module (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e2)). The free model and the divergence penalty measure or penalize $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}$ and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}$ computed as in Chapters 1, 2 and 5. The final projection and the projected flow apply the Leray projector of Chapter 6, either once at the end of generation or at each step of the flow. The potential parametrization generates the stream function $\psi$ and the magnetic potential $a$, then differentiates, as in Chapter 4. Since the fields of E2 are represented directly by their Fourier coefficients on a periodic grid, differentiation and projection are mode-by-mode operations there, exactly as in Chapters 5 and 6. The [taxonomy of constraints](../../rapport/index.html#taxonomie) in the report classifies these choices according to where they act: architecture, loss or sampling. In 3D, the direct generalization of the stream function is the vector potential, with the question of the gauge (Proposition 4.8 and Exercise 15); the divergence-free-by-construction networks of Richter-Powell et al. (2022) are another realization of it.

**Energy budget.** Proposition 3.10 and Exercise 8 give the magnetic and kinetic budgets; their sum makes the exchange term $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{B})\rangle$ disappear. In a statistically stationary regime, the average of the time derivative of the energy is zero, so that the injected power equals, on average, the sum of the viscous and Ohmic dissipations. This equality concerns the **distribution** of the fields, not each individual field: this is the meaning of the “distributional” energy budget constraint studied in the second part of experiment E2. The theoretical framework is set out in the [formulation](../../rapport/index.html#formulation) section of the report.

**Metrics.** The shell energy spectrum (Definition 5.13) rests on Parseval's identity. The kinetic helicity $\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\rangle$ is computed directly; the magnetic helicity requires a vector potential, and it is gauge invariant only in the periodic case or if $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$ on the boundary (Proposition 4.10). The divergence must be measured with the discrete operator that was used to impose it, and normalized (Remark 6.7). “Topology” refers to field lines, flux tubes (Section 3.3) and their linking, of which helicity gives a measure: for two thin flux tubes, it is proportional to their linking number (Moffatt, 1969). Zero helicity does not, however, imply the absence of linking.

**The three experiments of the repository.** Experiment E3 computes the growth rate of the kinematic dynamo driven by the ABC flow (Example 1.10, Exercise 5) as a function of $Rm$, with a 3D pseudo-spectral scheme and the 2/3 rule of Chapter 5 (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e3)). The induction equation is written there in curl form, $\partial_t\mathbf{B} = \nabla\times(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}) + \eta\Delta\mathbf{B}$: the divergence of $\mathbf{B}$ stays zero at the discrete level, thanks to the identity $\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{k}\times\hat{\mathbf{v}}) = 0$ of Section 5.5, which is the discrete version of Proposition 2.6. Experiment E1 deals with the three-mode model of Gissinger (2012), which has no spatial structure; this module enters it through a single remark: the induction equation is linear in $\mathbf{B}$ and the Lorentz force is quadratic, so that the MHD equations are invariant under $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$. This is the origin of the symmetry $(Q, D, V) \to (-Q, -D, V)$ of the model, where $Q$ and $D$ are amplitudes of magnetic modes and $V$ a velocity mode (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e1)).

**Toward the PhD.** The three experiments take place in a periodic domain or in low dimension, whereas the experimental dynamos VKS and DRESDYN are cylinders with walls. Section 6.3 explains why the projection there becomes a global Poisson problem, with nonlocal magnetic conditions; this is one of the open questions of the [PhD proposal](../../these/index.html#theorie), whose [experimental plan](../../these/index.html#plan-experimental) provides for a gradual transition from periodic to bounded geometries.

The natural next step in the pathway is the module [Fluid mechanics and turbulence](../p2-mecanique-fluides/index.html), which uses Parseval and spectra for the energy cascade, followed by the module [Electromagnetism, MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html), which starts from the induction equation of Section 2.3. The modules [Generative models: diffusion and flow matching](../p7-modeles-generatifs/index.html) and [Generative models under physical constraints](../p8-contraintes-physiques/index.html) directly reuse the Leray projection and the potentials.

## Further reading {#plus-loin}

1. **D. Tong, *Vector Calculus*** (first-year lecture notes from Cambridge, freely available). Chapters 3 and 4 cover the operators, curvilinear coordinates and the integral theorems with many examples drawn from physics; Section 4.4.1 proves Stokes' theorem for a curved surface, which we took for granted.
2. **L. N. Trefethen (2000), *Spectral Methods in MATLAB*.** A short and very concrete book on spectral differentiation, its accuracy and aliasing, organized around small programs that are easy to translate into NumPy. It is the best follow-up to Chapter 5.
3. **C. Canuto, M. Y. Hussaini, A. Quarteroni and T. A. Zang (2006), *Spectral Methods: Fundamentals in Single Domains*.** The reference work on spectral methods, to be consulted for the elimination of aliasing and for the Chebyshev bases that replace Fourier when the domain has walls.
4. **A. J. Chorin and J. E. Marsden (1993), *A Mathematical Introduction to Fluid Mechanics*.** A rigorous and brief introduction to the Euler and Navier–Stokes equations, in which the Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition with walls and the projection method play a central role. It extends Chapter 6.
5. **H. K. Moffatt and E. Dormy (2019), *Self-Exciting Fluid Dynamos*.** The modern treatise on dynamo theory: poloidal–toroidal decomposition, helicity, kinematic dynamos. It is the bridge between this module and the module [Electromagnetism, MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html).
